title: The Rules of This Place
description: Fifteen small worlds with exact rules. Find the route, the winning move, or the reason a tempting plan cannot work.

questions.prompt: A toy robot faces north. It turns a quarter-turn right, then another quarter-turn right, without turning again. Which way does it face?
questions.hint: Follow the turns in sequence rather than treating them as alternatives.
questions.explanation: The first turn faces east; the second faces south.

questions.explanation: Four presses make two cancelling pairs. The remaining press leaves the lamp on.

questions.prompt: Two players take turns removing either one or two stones from a pile of five. Whoever takes the last stone wins. You move first. How many should you take to guarantee a win?
questions.hint: Leave a pile from which either reply can be answered by taking the rest.
questions.explanation: Taking two leaves three. If the opponent takes one you take two; if they take two you take one.

questions.prompt: One cup starts with 100 mL of milk, another with 100 mL of coffee. Move 10 mL of milk into the coffee and mix, then return 10 mL of that mixture to the first cup. With no losses and additive volumes, which comparison is correct?

choices.text: More milk is in the coffee
Milk in the coffee equals coffee in the milk
More coffee is in the milk
The answer depends on the stirring speed

questions.hint: Both cups finish with their original total volume.
questions.explanation: Each millilitre of coffee now in the first cup displaces one millilitre of its original milk. That missing milk must be in the second cup, so the exchanged amounts are equal.

questions.prompt: You have empty 3-litre and 5-litre jugs, a tap and a drain. One move fills a jug, empties it, or pours one into the other until the source is empty or the destination full. What is the fewest moves needed to leave exactly 4 litres in the 5-litre jug?
questions.hint: A partially filled smaller jug can make the larger jug give up just the amount you need.
questions.explanation: Fill 5, pour into 3, empty 3, pour the remaining 2 into 3, refill 5, then top up 3. That leaves 4 litres in the large jug after six moves; no shorter allowed sequence does.

questions.prompt: A keeper must ferry a fox, a goose and beans across a river. The boat carries the keeper and at most one item. Without the keeper, fox cannot share a bank with goose, nor goose with beans. All start together. What is the fewest one-way crossings needed?
questions.hint: Sometimes moving something back is necessary to make progress.
questions.explanation: Take goose across, return alone, take fox across, bring goose back, take beans across, return alone, then take goose across. These seven crossings are minimal under the stated rules.

questions.prompt: Nine counters look identical. Exactly one is heavier, and the other eight weigh the same. Using a balance with outcomes left heavier, right heavier or balanced, what is the fewest weighings that always finds the heavy counter?
questions.hint: Aim for a first weighing that divides the possibilities into equal-sized groups.
questions.explanation: Weigh three against three. The result identifies a group of three; weighing one of those against another identifies the heavy counter. One weighing has only three outcomes, not enough for nine possibilities.

questions.prompt: Four walkers take 1, 2, 7 and 10 minutes to cross a bridge. At most two cross at once, always carrying the single lamp. A pair takes the slower walker's time; return trips also need the lamp. All start together. What is the minimum time to get everyone across?
questions.hint: Compare using one fast escort repeatedly with letting the two slowest travel together.
questions.explanation: Send 1 and 2 across, return 1, send 7 and 10, return 2, then send 1 and 2. The total is 2 + 1 + 10 + 2 + 2 = 17 minutes, the optimal schedule.

questions.prompt: Two identical test orbs break when dropped above an unknown highest safe floor, which is an integer from 0 to 10. An unbroken orb is reusable; a broken one is lost. What is the fewest drops that can ALWAYS determine the highest safe floor?
questions.hint: After a break, only one orb remains, so lower untested floors may need checking one by one.
questions.explanation: With four drops and two orbs, test floors 4, 7, 9 and 10 if nothing breaks, checking intervening floors after a break. Three drops can distinguish at most seven possible thresholds, fewer than the eleven needed.

questions.prompt: Three coins start tails-up. Each move flips exactly two different coins. Can all three ever finish heads-up?

choices.text: No; the number of tails stays odd

questions.hint: A move changes the number of tails by either zero or two.
questions.explanation: Starting with three tails, flipping two coins preserves whether the tail count is odd or even. Zero tails is even, so it is unreachable.

questions.prompt: Remove two diagonally opposite corner squares from an 8-by-8 checkerboard. A domino covers two edge-adjacent remaining squares. What is the MAXIMUM number of dominoes that can be placed without overlap?
questions.hint: A domino always covers one square of each colour.
questions.explanation: The removed corners have the same colour, leaving colour counts 30 and 32, so at most 30 dominoes fit. Leaving one further square beside each removed corner allows all other squares to be tiled, achieving 30.

questions.prompt: There are three piles of 2, 4 and 7 stones. Players alternate taking any positive number from ONE pile; whoever takes the last stone wins. Both play perfectly. Which opening move guarantees the first player a win?
questions.hint: Think of pile sizes as groups of ones, twos and fours that can balance across piles.
questions.explanation: Leaving 2, 4 and 6 balances every binary place: each occurs in an even number of piles. Any opponent move breaks that balance, and you can restore it; this maintains a winning reply until the last stone.

questions.prompt: A corridor has rooms 1 through 12. From any room you may move exactly three rooms forward or two rooms back, but never leave the corridor. Starting in room 1, what is the fewest moves to reach room 12?
questions.hint: For a fixed number of moves, replacing a forward move with a backward move changes the total progress by five.
questions.explanation: A route is 1, 4, 7, 10, 8, 11, 9, 12. With n moves and b backwards, progress is 3n − 5b; reaching 11 rooms ahead first permits nonnegative whole counts at n = 7.

questions.prompt: Exactly one of 16 vials contains a dye. A test strip turns blue if and only if its sample contains any dye. You may mix samples from any vials on a strip, and test all strips in ONE batch. What is the fewest strips that always identifies the dyed vial?
questions.hint: Each strip adds a yes-or-no result; a pattern of results can identify a vial.
questions.explanation: Three strips give only eight result patterns, fewer than sixteen. Four give sixteen: assign each vial a different four-bit label and include its sample on precisely the strips marked 1; even all-negative results identify one vial.
